How to actually use it (read this bit) Here is the uncomfortable truth about maths revision: reading a worked solution feels like learning and mostly isn't. When you read someone else's solution, your brain goes "yes, obviously, I could have done that." That feeling is called fluency illusion and it is the single biggest reason people walk out of a maths exam surprised by their own grade. So the rule for every practice question on this site: Attempt the question on paper, fully, to an answer , before you open the solution. If you get stuck, note exactly where you got stuck, then open the solution and read only until you're unstuck. Close it. Finish the question yourself. A workable routine for one topic: 1. Read the explanation sections properly once. Slowly. Pen in hand. 2. Cover each worked example's solution and try it first. Then compare, line by line. 3. Why this topic exists Someone claims a coin is fair. You flip it 20 times and get 15 heads. Is that evidence of bias, or just luck? Hypothesis testing answers exactly this. If not, you have insufficient evidence against . - Null hypothesis : the "no change / no effect" claim, always with an equals sign ( ). - Alternative hypothesis : what you're testing for ( , , or ). - Significance level : the threshold, typically 5% or 1%. t: Building a Revision Plan That Works
k: The honest starting point Most maths revision fails for one reason: it feels like work without being work. Re-reading notes, copying out worked examples, highlighting a textbook, watching videos — all of these produce the warm sensation of understanding and almost none of the ability to produce an answer under pressure. You've been shown the method. You haven't retrieved it. The techniques below are less comfortable and considerably more effective. That trade is the whole thing. --- 1. The four principles 1. Retrieval practice. Closing the book and producing the method from memory. This is the single most effective study technique there is, and it's the one that feels worst, because you keep failing during it. The failing is the mechanism. 2. Spacing. Revisiting a topic after a gap, repeatedly, rather than hammering it once. Four 20-minute sessions across a month beat one 80-minute session, by a wide margin. 3. Interleaving. Mixing topics within a session. It feels chaotic and produces worse practice performance — and substantially better exam performance, because exams don't tell you which method to use. Mixed practice is how you learn to choose . 4. Error logging. Recording every dropped mark and why. Your error log is the most personalised, highest-value revision document you will ever own. Re-reading is easy because the information is right there. Retrieval is hard because you have to generate it. But generating it is what builds the retrieval path — and the exam is a retrieval task, not a recognition task. This is called desirable difficulty . If your revision feels smooth and pleasant, it's probably not doing much. If it feels effortful and you keep getting stuck, that's the sensation of learning. The practical implication: judge a revision session by how much you produced , not by how much you covered . --- 2. A structure for the two years During Year 12 and 13 (ongoing) - After each new topic: do the practice questions on that topic's page here, cold, on paper. - Three days later: redo the two you got wrong. This one habit is worth more than any amount of end-of-year cramming. - Every few weeks: a mixed set of 6–8 questions drawn from different topics. Six months out - Work through every topic once, in order, doing the practice questions. - Build your formula sheet (see EX1) and start testing yourself on it weekly. - Start your error log .
